# 研究任务：自动调优之后，报告的基准分数意味着什么

## 背景与动机

在大语言模型（LLM）的实际使用中，研究者常常在一个基准的题目上自动搜索提示词（prompt）
或由多个 LLM 调用组成的程序（pipeline），再把搜索得到的"最佳配置"在同一批题目上的得分
作为该系统的性能汇报。所用的自动搜索工具多种多样。

这种做法引出一个统计问题：基准题目既被用来**挑选**配置，又被用来给该配置**打分**，因此
汇报的数字不一定反映系统在全新题目上的真实表现；基于这类汇报数字做出的比较和决定是否
可靠，也就不清楚。

## 研究问题

请围绕下面的问题开展一项完整的研究：

1. 对一个先在有限题集上搜索配置、再把选出的配置拿去使用的系统，汇报的分数与它在全新
   题目上的真实表现相差多少？差距受哪些因素影响？它是否会影响基于汇报分数做出的结论？
2. 能否设计更可靠的汇报方式？应如何通过实验检验它是否可靠？

## 成功如何衡量

结论需要有你自己运行的实验支持，并至少在一个真实 LLM 与真实基准的设置上检验；实验设计、
统计工具和理论分析的深度由你决定。结论可以是支持、反驳或视条件而定。

# Brief — what is a benchmark score worth after the configuration was tuned on that benchmark?
(v2, after idea review 1: estimands per protocol, leakage re-specified, compute arithmetic, priorities, null cases, near work.)

## Question
A prompt or LLM pipeline is searched on a finite set S of n benchmark items; the best configuration's score **on S** is reported. We ask:
1. **Size and drivers of the gap** between that report and the selected configuration's accuracy on fresh items of the same benchmark: dependence on n, search budget/space (K and how similar the configurations are), spread of true configuration quality σ_θ, search algorithm, and items placed in the prompt. Does the gap change **decisions** drawn from reported scores (tuned-vs-untuned gains, tuned-A-vs-tuned-B rankings, significance)?
2. **Reliable reporting.** Which reporting protocols are valid and how efficient, tested with ground truth.

The lead contribution is an **evidence-based answer** (size, drivers, which protocols are valid, where a cheap search-log bound works and where it fails), not a claim to have been first to notice the gap.

## Position (what prior work leaves open)
Selection bias after model selection (Cawley & Talbot 2010; Tibshirani & Tibshirani 2009; Efron & Tibshirani 1997), simultaneous post-selection bounds for the *same-sample* select-and-assess setting (Rink & Brannath 2025 — the closest to our max-t candidate), inference on winners (Andrews et al.), adaptive reuse (Dwork et al.; Blum & Hardt), Gaussian-max theory (Chernozhukov et al.). Empirical meta-analyses (Roelofs 2019, Recht 2019) find little adaptive overfitting for leaderboard rankings, so size is an empirical question. LLM-side work measures prompt sensitivity (Sclar; Polo; option-order/selection-bias work of Zheng, Pezeshkpour) or builds searchers (APE, OPRO, ProTeGi, DSPy/MIPRO, GEPA, Shi et al.) and reports the optimised score. What we add, hedged to our reading of the literature: a controlled ground-truth measurement for searched LLM configurations at benchmark scale, its drivers expressed through quantities observable in the search log (σ_θ, effective number of competing configurations), decision-level consequences with explicit null scenarios, an equal-item-budget head-to-head of reporting protocols, and an honest test of where a search-log bound (item-level matrix, correlated configurations) breaks (adaptive/nested-subset search). Positioning is re-checked at each release.
The answer may be conditional: expected (to be tested) — a few points of optimism at n ≲ a few hundred with many near-equivalent configurations; negligible at n in the thousands or when σ_θ ≫ noise. If real-LLM gaps are small in realistic regimes, that is the finding, with the regimes where they are not.

## Priority order (what is cut first when compute falls short: from the bottom)
1. **Lead — real MMLU-Pro matrix:** gap vs (n, K_eff, σ_θ) with random search and the grid searchers, plus decision-level consequences (incl. null scenarios) and the verification-noise floor.
2. **Head-to-head of reporting protocols** at equal N_tot: naive, split, nested CV/cross-fit, optimism bootstrap, Šidák/Bonferroni, max-t bound.
3. **Semi-synthetic/synthetic arm** (cheap, CPU): drivers isolated, regimes beyond real n and K, failure regimes; calibrated to the real matrix (low-rank/IRT fit incl. subject structure).
4. DSPy/real-tool confirmatory arm (short).
5. Extras: Andrews hybrid/conditional, Ladder/Thresholdout, empirical-Bayes shrinkage, a second model, leakage counterfactual extension.

# Prior work and how the study relates to it

Only works whose title/abstract or full text was consulted via the literature search are listed; links are from OpenAlex/arXiv/DOI records. The single published paper on this exact question named in the objective was not searched for or read.

## Selection bias and adaptive reuse of data (the statistical core)
- Cawley & Talbot, *On over-fitting in model selection and subsequent selection bias in performance evaluation*, JMLR 2010. https://doi.org/10.5555/1756006.1859921 — closest classical analogue (selection criterion = performance estimate; reported best score biased). Relation: we study the same bias for prompt/pipeline configurations, add item-in-prompt leakage and decision-level consequences.
- Tibshirani & Tibshirani, *A bias correction for the minimum error rate in cross-validation*, AoAS 2009. https://doi.org/10.1214/08-aoas224 — bias estimate for the minimum CV error; a baseline correction we compare with.
- Rink & Brannath, *Post-selection confidence bounds for prediction performance*, Machine Learning 2025. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-024-06632-w — (abstract read) simultaneous confidence bounds for the selected model when selection and evaluation use the same sample; closest to our max-t candidate. Relation: we adapt this idea to item-level correlated outcomes from LLM search logs, test it under adaptive and nested-subset search, and compare it at equal item budget with splits, nested CV and bootstrap; the new part is the LLM-search setting and its empirical validity map, not the idea of a simultaneous bound.
- Efron & Tibshirani, *Improvements on cross-validation: the .632+ bootstrap method*, JASA 1997. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1997.10474007 — origin of the optimism-bootstrap family; baseline.
- Test-error estimation after model selection from validation errors (arXiv:1801.02817, abstract read) — another correction for the minimum validation error; related baseline.
- Varma & Simon 2006: not located by the literature search, dropped from the citation list until verified.
- Bates, Hastie & Tibshirani, *Cross-validation: what does it estimate and how well does it do it?*, JASA 2023. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2023.2197686 — CV estimates the procedure's error, not that of the fitted model; justifies the "procedure vs selected configuration" distinction in reporting.
- Dwork et al., *Preserving statistical validity in adaptive data analysis*, STOC 2015, arXiv:1411.2664; *The reusable holdout*, Science 2015, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaa9375; Blum & Hardt, *The Ladder*, ICML 2015, arXiv:1502.04585 — theory/mechanisms for adaptive reuse of a holdout; Ladder/Thresholdout are baselines. Relation: worst-case/mechanism-design vs our measured gap for real LLM search and a cheap post-hoc bound.
- Roelofs et al., *A meta-analysis of overfitting in machine learning*, NeurIPS 2019; Recht et al., *Do ImageNet classifiers generalize to ImageNet?*, ICML 2019 (arXiv:1902.10811) — empirical adaptive overfitting at the benchmark/leaderboard level (small for rankings, large absolute drops under distribution shift). Relation: tells us a small effect is possible; we measure the effect at the level of a single searched configuration and separate it from distribution shift (we use fresh items from the same pool).
- Andrews, Kitagawa & McCloskey, *Inference on winners*, QJE 2024 (NBER w25456). https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjad043 — conditional/hybrid confidence intervals and median-unbiased estimates after selecting the best of K; baselines (adapted to correlated binary outcomes).
